author: Paul Grondahl
title: Grondahl: Albany Firefighters Museum eyes old Trailways bus station - NewsBreak
text:
By Paul Grondahl ,
18 hours ago Architect Jack Waite said the 1965 Mid-Century Modern former Adirondack Trailways bus station, which has been abandoned since the 1990s, has a steel frame, is structurally sound and can be restored at a reasonable price. (Paul Grondahl/For the Times Union) ALBANY — The Albany Firefighters Museum at 384 Broadway downtown has run out of room and needs a larger space to display a historic firetruck undergoing restoration.
Organizers believe the solution lies at the end of the block at 358 Broadway and the long-abandoned Adirondack Trailways bus station. Museum leaders are rallying support and preparing to apply for grants as part of Gov. Kathy Hochul’s $200 million investment into the revitalization of downtown.
It would more than quadruple the museum’s space.
“It’s always been a dream of mine to move into that building,” said Bill Tobler, who worked in each of the city’s firehouses during a 39-year career with the Albany Fire Department. He retired in 2012 and teamed up with Albany historian Tony Opalka and architect Jack Waite to launch the Albany Firefighters Museum.
“Call it a vision, not a dream,” Waite said as the three men stood outside the former Trailways bus station, which gleamed in Sunday’s afternoon sun. “This building is in good shape structurally. It’s worth saving. We’re just lucky it wasn’t torn down.”
Preservationists got the building listed on the National Register of Historic Places, which delayed demolition.
Built in 1965 in the Mid-Century Modern style, it has been vacant for decades. (Trailways initially moved its operations to the nearby Greyhound bus station before decamping in 2022 to a temporary location, a trailer at 66 Green St.)
The 358 Broadway building was slated to be torn down as part of a Capitalize Albany Corp. plan to build a convention center as the centerpiece of redevelopment of the eight-acre Liberty Park site known as the “parking lot district.” That plan was pared down, and the Albany Capital Center was built several blocks away.
The derelict Trailways bus station deteriorated over the years as water poured in from a damaged roof. Tentative plans for restoration and reuse, which ranged from office space to a restaurant, came and went like the tides on the Hudson River.
Waite, founder of John G. Waite Associates, watched with disappointment as the building fell into disrepair. His architectural firm specializes in preservation and occupies the historic R.B. Wing and Son building at 384 Broadway.
In 2023, Capitalize Albany Corp. received a $356,000 state grant to stabilize the two-story building by making roof repairs aimed at stopping water damage.
Waite’s late father, John G. Waite Sr., was a captain in the Troy Fire Department. Waite keeps his father’s firefighting gear in his office and collects firefighting artifacts. Waite’s firm worked on the restoration of three historic firehouses in Albany. He was a catalyst for the creation of the not-for-profit Albany Firefighters Museum in 2014 to mark the 150th anniversary of professional fire service in the city. Waite has provided a ground-level space at his firm’s building for the museum, which it has outgrown.
In the former Trailways terminal, Waite envisions the large portico where buses used to pull beneath enclosed in glass to display historic fire equipment. The centerpiece would be a 1921 American LaFrance firetruck that was one of the Albany Fire Department’s original six motorized fire engines. It was in service at Engine No. 1 near Washington Park.
Museum leaders purchased it in 2022. It is being restored in Cambridge by a volunteer, Howard Schmitt Jr., son of the late Battalion Chief Howard R. Schmitt.
“The 1921 American LaFrance will be a major addition to the museum,” said Opalka, author of an exhaustively researched and illustrated coffee table book, “The Firehouses of Albany.” The book is in its third printing, an indicator of the interest in the city’s firefighting history.
If successful in restoring the former Trailways building, museum organizers plan to display three historic pieces of fire equipment on extended loan at the State Museum’s Fire Engine Hall: a 1926 American LaFrance 65-foot, tractor-drawn water tower and two early steam engine firetrucks.
“Kids love seeing firetrucks and we would bring them to parades and display them so families could come and enjoy them,” Tobler said. “Our museum is a slice of American history and the role that the firefighting service played in Albany.”
Opalka’s book traces that history to 1732, when the city purchased its first fire engine, followed in 1763 by the appointment of the first firemen and the Common Council’s codification of the duties of firefighters.
“Council minutes from the 1760s stated that firefighting was considered the most important service in the development of the city,” Opalka said.
The Great Albany Fire on Aug. 17, 1848, killed 10 people and injured dozens, destroyed nearly 600 buildings, devastating the city’s commercial core. The fire started in a stable at Broadway and Herkimer Street and blazed for hours, spread by strong winds. At the time, the city relied on an all-volunteer fire department. After the fire, the city shifted to a paid fire department and established strict building codes to prevent future fire catastrophes.
Waite, Tobler and Opalka are speaking with city officials and laying the groundwork to apply for restoration funds from Hochul’s $200 million downtown redevelopment initiative.
“This isn’t a pipe dream. There’s no question the building can be restored and at a reasonable price,” said Waite, who could not provide a cost estimate at this point.
Museum organizers want to build upon Historic Albany Foundation’s restoration of the city’s oldest building, the 1728 Van Ostrande-Radliff House at 48 Hudson Ave., two blocks from the former Trailways bus station.
“That’s an important new addition for cultural tourism,” Waite said. “We’ve got the USS Slater nearby. Together with the Albany Firefighters Museum and the state’s $150 million investment in the State Museum, there is a lot of positive momentum. If the Albany Waterway group can restore Lock 1 of the Erie Canal to the north, it would be a terrific corridor of historic sites and museums.”
Waite credited his mentor at the RPI School of Architecture, Dean Bernd Foerster, an early advocate of historic preservation, with a passion for saving old buildings, even those built in the 1960s.
“Mid-Century Modern buildings were looked down upon and called intrusions for a long time,” Waite said. “That was not the fault of the buildings, it was the fault of short-sighted architects.”
Paul Grondahl is the Opalka Endowed Director of the New York State Writers Institute at the University at Albany and a former Times Union reporter. He can be reached at grondahlpaul@gmail.com
